solution.concept_anchor: NGT statutory vs constitutional body distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who recall that the NGT derives philosophical support from Article 21 and Article 48A may incorrectly conflate philosophical underpinning with constitutional establishment.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): NGT is not established by any constitutional provision — no article of the Constitution creates it directly.
Eliminate (c): The NHRC is established under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993, making it also statutory, but it is not the body in question here.
Eliminate (d): The Central Pollution Control Board is established under the Water Act 1974, not the NGT Act — entirely different body.
Confirm (b): The NGT was constituted through the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 — a parliamentary statute — making it a statutory tribunal.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A common exam trap is to confuse bodies that draw philosophical support from constitutional provisions with bodies that are constitutionally established. The NGT invokes Article 21 (right to a healthy environment) and Article 48A (Directive Principle on environment protection) as its normative basis, but it was created by Parliament through the NGT Act 2010 — not by the Constitution itself. Students who loosely recall the Article 21 connection may mark (a) without recognising the distinction between philosophical underpinning and formal establishment.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Green Tribunal is a creature of ordinary parliamentary legislation, not the Constitution of India. It was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, placing it in the same category as other statutory tribunals rather than constitutionally mandated bodies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No article of the Constitution directly creates the NGT. Articles 21 and 48A provide the normative justification for environmental protection but do not constitute the tribunal.
• Option (b) — Correct: The NGT Act 2010 is the parent statute; Parliament enacted it to provide speedy environmental justice.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The NHRC is established under the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 — also statutory, but a different body entirely.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CPCB is established under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, not the NGT Act.

Value Addition:
• Australia's Land and Environment Court (NSW, 1980) is considered a global parallel to India's NGT as a specialised environmental tribunal.
• Art. 48A (DPSP) directs the State to protect and improve the environment — often cited in NGT preamble reasoning.
• Being statutory means Parliament can amend or dissolve the NGT by simple legislative majority, unlike constitutional bodies.

concepts_used: Original Jurisdiction of NGT
Suo Motu Powers — Absence and its Significance

solution.concept_anchor: NGT original jurisdiction locus standi and suo motu absence

statement_analysis.statement: Any person, irrespective of whether they are directly aggrieved, can file an application before the NGT invoking its original jurisdiction.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT Act provides a broad locus standi — 'any person' may approach the tribunal, unlike conventional civil courts that require the petitioner to demonstrate personal aggrievement.

statement_analysis.statement: The NGT can take suo motu cognizance of environmental violations reported in newspaper articles, similar to the power exercised by the Supreme Court under Article 32.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike the Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226), the NGT is not empowered to take suo motu cognizance — it can only act on a petition or application filed before it.

statement_analysis.statement: The original jurisdiction of the NGT is exercisable only in relation to substantial questions touching the environment under the Acts listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14 of the NGT Act limits original jurisdiction to substantial environmental questions arising under the seven scheduled Acts — NGT cannot entertain matters beyond this list.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) which would include Statement 2 tempts students who correctly know Statements 1 and 3 are true but erroneously believe NGT has suo motu powers because they associate environmental urgency with expansive judicial powers.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 'Any person' filing is explicitly provided — locus standi is wide; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Suo motu power belongs to constitutional courts — NGT requires a petition; Statement 2 is incorrect, eliminate any option including it as correct.
Verify Statement 3: Schedule I limitation on original jurisdiction is a well-established feature of Section 14; Statement 3 is correct.
Only option (b) — Statements 1 and 3 only — matches this verdict.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who are aware of the Supreme Court's activist suo motu practice in environmental matters (Art. 32 PILs) may wrongly attribute the same power to the NGT, especially since NGT deals with the same subject matter. The trap here is the scope-extension fallacy — just because a body is specialised in environment does not mean it possesses the full suite of judicial powers that constitutional courts enjoy. The NGT's dependence on applications being filed is a structural limitation, not an oversight.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT's original jurisdiction is governed by Section 14 of the NGT Act. Understanding who can approach it, on what subject matter, and through what mechanism is fundamental to NGT questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Act adopts an expansive standing rule — 'any person' may file, which includes NGOs, individuals, and community groups without needing to show direct harm.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The NGT cannot act suo motu. It is entirely petition-driven. This contrasts sharply with the Supreme Court's Art. 32 power and High Courts' Art. 226 power, both of which allow self-initiated action.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Original jurisdiction is confined to substantial questions of environment under the seven Acts in Schedule I. Matters under statutes outside this list (e.g., Wildlife Protection Act 1972) cannot be entertained under original jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• The lack of suo motu power is a frequently cited criticism of the NGT — delays in filing can render environmental damage irreversible.
• The seven Schedule I Acts include EPA 1986, Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Forest Conservation Act 1980, Biological Diversity Act 2002, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, and National Environment Tribunal Act 1995.
• 'Substantial question relating to environment' is a threshold requirement — trivial or technical disputes may not meet this bar.

concepts_used: Appellate Jurisdiction of NGT
Limitation Period for Filing Applications before NGT

solution.concept_anchor: NGT appellate jurisdiction time limits

statement_analysis.statement: An appeal against an order passed by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority must be filed before the NGT within 60 days of the impugned order.
statement_analysis.reason: The prescribed limitation period for appellate applications before the NGT is 30 days from the impugned order (not 60 days) — 60 days is the additional period of condonable delay, not the primary period.

statement_analysis.statement: The NGT's appellate jurisdiction extends to orders and decisions of all statutory environmental authorities, regardless of whether the underlying statute is listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Appellate jurisdiction is restricted to orders passed under the Schedule I Acts — not all environmental statutory authorities are covered; decisions under non-scheduled Acts (e.g., WPA 1972) cannot be appealed to the NGT.

statement_analysis.statement: An original application before the NGT must be filed within 5 years from the date on which the cause of action first arose.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 14(3) of the NGT Act prescribes a 5-year limitation for original applications — this is distinct from the 30-day limit applicable to appellate matters.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong but mistakenly believe Statement 3 is also wrong (confusing the 5-year original period with the appellate 30-day period) will choose (b), missing that only Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Primary appellate limitation is 30 days, not 60 — 60 days is the maximum extension period; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Appellate jurisdiction is tied to Schedule I Acts only — orders under non-scheduled statutes cannot be appealed to NGT; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The 5-year limitation for original applications is correctly stated per Section 14(3); Statement 3 is correct.
The question asks which are NOT correct — Statements 1 and 2 are not correct; answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 60-day figure is a legitimate number in the NGT framework — it is the maximum additional period by which the tribunal can condone delay beyond the primary 30-day window. Students who recall '60 days' in connection with appellate filings often misplace it as the primary limitation, not realising it is only the outer boundary of condonable delay. This temporal-swap trap is highly effective because both 30 and 60 are real numbers within the same statutory provision.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT operates under two distinct limitation regimes — one for original applications (Section 14) and one for appeals (Section 16). Conflating these is a common and costly exam error.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The initial limitation for appeals is 30 days from the date of the impugned order. The tribunal may condone delay for up to a further 60 days if sufficient cause is shown — but 60 days is not the primary period.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Appellate jurisdiction is not universal. Only orders/decisions under the seven Schedule I Acts can be appealed to the NGT. Decisions of authorities acting under non-scheduled statutes like the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 fall outside this appellate route.
• Statement 3 — Correct: For original applications under Section 14, the limitation is 5 years from the date of the first arising of the cause of action, with a discretionary power to condone delay.

Value Addition:
• SEIAA (State Environment Impact Assessment Authority) functions under the EPA 1986 — a Schedule I Act — so its orders are appealable to NGT.
• The 30+60 day appellate window mirrors procedural safeguards in civil litigation while ensuring environmental disputes are resolved swiftly.
• Delay condonation beyond 90 days total requires exceptional justification and is not routine.

Exclusion of Wildlife Protection Act and Its Implications

solution.concept_anchor: NGT Schedule I Acts — inclusions and exclusions

statement_analysis.statement: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Water Act 1974 is one of the seven Acts listed in Schedule I, giving NGT jurisdiction over matters arising under it.

statement_analysis.statement: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 is listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is specifically excluded from Schedule I — this is a classic NGT trap and means NGT cannot directly adjudicate disputes arising purely under WPA.

statement_analysis.statement: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 is among the seven scheduled Acts, allowing NGT to hear disputes relating to biodiversity conservation and access and benefit sharing.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Forest Act, 1927 is listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian Forest Act 1927 is not included in Schedule I. Only the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 is scheduled — a common source of exam confusion between the two forest-related statutes.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify WPA 1972 as excluded but mistakenly believe the Indian Forest Act 1927 is scheduled, thus counting three correct pairings.
elimination_logic: Pair 1 (Water Act 1974): Clearly a Schedule I Act — mark correct.
Pair 2 (Wildlife Protection Act 1972): A well-known exclusion from Schedule I — mark incorrect.
Pair 3 (Biological Diversity Act 2002): Included in Schedule I — mark correct.
Pair 4 (Indian Forest Act 1927): Only the Forest Conservation Act 1980 is in Schedule I, not the 1927 Act — mark incorrect. Two correct pairings total → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate simultaneously here. First, students confuse the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 (not scheduled) with the Forest Conservation Act 1980 (scheduled) — both deal with natural resources. Second, students confuse the Indian Forest Act 1927 (not scheduled) with the Forest Conservation Act 1980 (scheduled) — the names sound related and both involve forests. A student aware of the WPA trap but unaware of the IFA trap will arrive at three correct pairs instead of two, selecting (c) instead of (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Schedule I of the NGT Act defines the outer boundary of the tribunal's jurisdiction. Knowing precisely which Acts are included — and which are excluded — is essential for NGT questions.

The seven Acts in Schedule I are: (1) Water Act 1974, (2) Water (Cess) Act 1977, (3) Air Act 1981, (4) Environment Protection Act 1986, (5) Forest Conservation Act 1980, (6) Biological Diversity Act 2002, (7) Public Liability Insurance Act 1991.

• Pair 1 (Water Act 1974) — Correct: Clearly listed.
• Pair 2 (Wildlife Protection Act 1972) — Incorrect: Not in Schedule I; High Courts retain writ jurisdiction for pure WPA matters.
• Pair 3 (Biological Diversity Act 2002) — Correct: Listed, enabling NGT to hear ABS and conservation disputes.
• Pair 4 (Indian Forest Act 1927) — Incorrect: This pre-independence statute is not scheduled; only the Forest Conservation Act 1980 is.

Value Addition:
• NGT can still address wildlife-adjacent issues if they involve EPA 1986 or Forest Conservation Act 1980 overlaps.
• The National Environment Tribunal Act 1995 is also in Schedule I, though it is now largely superseded by NGT itself.
• Exclusion of WPA 1972 means poaching, wildlife trade, and sanctuary violations must be taken to criminal courts or High Courts.

Principal Bench and its Location

solution.concept_anchor: NGT zonal bench locations and territorial coverage
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly places the Eastern Bench at Kolkata but swaps Western (Pune) with Central (Bhopal) and Southern, tempting students who know two of the four locations but guess on the remaining pair.
elimination_logic: Principal Bench is definitively at New Delhi — anchor A-4 to eliminate options misplacing it.
Southern Bench is at Chennai — anchor B-3 and eliminate options placing it at Pune or Bhopal.
Central Bench is at Bhopal — anchor C-1 and cross-check options.
Western Bench is at Pune — anchor D-2; only option (c) satisfies all four matches correctly.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap exploits the fact that students often know two or three of the four bench locations with certainty but guess the remaining one. Pune and Bhopal are the most commonly swapped pair — Pune sounds 'Central' given Maharashtra's geographic position, while Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh) is the actual Central Bench location. The Southern Bench at Chennai is relatively well-known, but the Northeast gap (no dedicated bench there) is an additional conceptual trap embedded in the broader topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT operates through a Principal Bench and four Zonal Benches, each serving a defined territorial jurisdiction across Indian states.

Correct matches:
• A (Southern Bench) — 3 (Chennai): The Southern Bench covers states including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
• B (Western Bench) — 2 (Pune): The Western Bench covers Maharashtra, Goa, Gujarat, and neighbouring states.
• C (Central Bench) — 1 (Bhopal): The Central Bench covers Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and others.
• D (Principal Bench) — 4 (New Delhi): The Chairperson sits here; it has pan-India jurisdiction for unassigned matters.

The Eastern Bench is at Kolkata — covering West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar, Jharkhand, and northeastern states (no separate Northeast bench exists).

Value Addition:
• NGT can hold Circuit Bench sittings at locations other than the four Zonal Bench cities for convenience of litigants.
• The northeast coverage gap through Kolkata bench has been a subject of access-to-justice debates.
• All appeals from Zonal Bench orders in certain matters can be routed through the Principal Bench.

Relationship Between NGT and High Courts — Jurisdictional Overlap

solution.concept_anchor: NGT appeals bypassing High Courts to Supreme Court
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may reflexively choose (a) without questioning whether R actually explains A, since 'preventing forum shopping' sounds like a perfectly logical reason for bypassing High Courts.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. NGT orders are appealable directly to the Supreme Court, bypassing all High Courts — this is expressly provided in the NGT Act.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Preventing multiplicity of proceedings and forum shopping in multiple High Courts is a recognised rationale cited in parliamentary debates on the NGT Act.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The direct appeal to the Supreme Court is not a consequence of preventing forum shopping; it is a structural design choice grounded in the fact that NGT is a national tribunal with pan-India jurisdiction, making a single apex appellate forum appropriate. Forum shopping prevention is a beneficial effect, not the operative constitutional or statutory cause.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are factually accurate statements about the NGT appeal hierarchy. The trap is causal — R sounds like a convincing reason for A because preventing forum shopping is indeed an advantage of routing appeals directly to the Supreme Court. However, the correct explanation for bypassing High Courts is institutional design: NGT is a national-level body with all-India jurisdiction, and having its orders potentially reviewed by 25 different High Courts would create jurisprudential inconsistency. Forum shopping prevention is an incidental benefit, not the driving causal rationale codified in the statute.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT creates a unique appellate hierarchy in Indian law — one of the few tribunals whose orders bypass the High Court tier entirely.

Assertion (A): Correct. Section 22 of the NGT Act provides that any person aggrieved by an order of the NGT may file an appeal to the Supreme Court within 90 days. No intermediate High Court review is contemplated.

Reason (R): Correct as a factual claim. Preventing forum shopping — where litigants strategically choose favourable High Courts — was indeed discussed as a benefit of centralised appellate review during the NGT Act's legislative history.

Causal link: R does NOT explain A. The primary reason for direct Supreme Court appeals is that the NGT is a national tribunal exercising jurisdiction across all states. A national body's orders logically require a national apex forum. If each zonal bench's orders went to the respective High Court, it would fragment environmental jurisprudence and create conflicting precedents. Forum shopping prevention is an effect of this design, not its cause.

Value Addition:
• The 90-day window for Supreme Court appeal from an NGT order is itself a substantial period given environmental urgency considerations.
• A similar direct-to-Supreme-Court structure exists for bodies like the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) on certain matters.
• High Courts retain Art. 226 jurisdiction but typically defer to NGT as the specialised forum.

concepts_used: Composition of NGT — Judicial and Expert Members

solution.concept_anchor: NGT composition qualification requirements
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the qualification threshold for expert members as 'minimum 10 years' instead of 15 years — a plausible figure that mirrors the judicial member minimum count.
elimination_logic: The Chairperson must be a retired Supreme Court Judge — this is the most senior position, placing it at the apex of qualification requirements.
Judicial Members must be retired High Court Judges — subordinate to Chairperson qualification, placing them at the second tier.
Expert Members require a doctorate OR 15 years' professional experience in environmental/forest/science fields — not 10 years; eliminate any option citing 10 years.
The minimum count for both Judicial and Expert Members is 10 each (maximum 20 each) — confirming option (d).
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT's composition reflects its interdisciplinary mandate — environmental adjudication requires both legal expertise and scientific/technical knowledge.

• Option (a): Incorrect — The Chairperson must be a retired Supreme Court Judge, not a sitting judge. A serving judge cannot hold a tribunal position simultaneously.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Expert Members must have 15 years of experience (or a doctorate), not 10 years. The figure 10 relates to the minimum number of members, not the experience threshold.
• Option (c): Incorrect — The maximum number of Judicial Members and Expert Members is 20 each, not 15. Confusing the experience threshold (15 years) with the maximum membership (20) is a common error.
• Option (d): Correct — Chairperson is a retired Supreme Court Judge; Judicial Members are retired High Court Judges; Expert Members need a doctorate or 15 years' experience; both categories have a floor of 10 and ceiling of 20 members.

Value Addition:
• The mandatory expert member presence distinguishes NGT from ordinary civil courts, enabling in-house evaluation of pollution data and environmental impact reports.
• A bench without an expert member is not validly constituted under the NGT Act.
• The multidisciplinary design mirrors the approach of Australia's Land and Environment Court, which also uses specialist commissioners.

Penalty for Non-Compliance with NGT Orders

solution.concept_anchor: NGT civil compensation powers vs criminal imprisonment scope
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that the NGT Act contains an imprisonment provision may incorrectly apply it to the underlying environmental violation itself, rather than recognising it applies only to non-compliance with NGT orders.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a violation causing environmental damage — NGT's response power is to award compensation and order restoration; identify this as the primary remedy.
Check whether NGT can impose imprisonment for the pollution violation itself — it cannot; imprisonment under NGT Act applies to non-compliance with orders, not to the act of pollution.
Eliminate (c): Imprisonment for the pollution act is a criminal law remedy — NGT is a civil tribunal and cannot impose criminal sentences for the underlying offence.

Eliminate (b) and (d): There is no monetary cap on compensation NGT can award, and NGT can also order environmental restoration simultaneously with compensation — option (a) correctly captures both powers.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The NGT Act does provide for imprisonment — but only for non-compliance with NGT orders (up to 3 years), not for the original environmental violation. Students who recall the imprisonment provision without remembering its precise trigger will apply it to the pollution act itself, choosing option (c). This scope-extension trap exploits partial knowledge of the Act's penalty provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
A petrochemical company discharges untreated effluents into a river, violating conditions under an environmental clearance granted under the Environment Protection Act, 1986. Residents file an application before the NGT.

Applicable principles: As a civil tribunal, the NGT can award compensation to affected persons (polluter pays principle) and order restoration of the damaged ecosystem. There is no upper monetary cap on compensation, unlike consumer forums. The NGT can also order the creation of restoration funds managed by a designated authority.

• Option (a) — Correct: The NGT can award compensation to victims (no cap) and simultaneously direct environmental restoration — both remedies are available under the NGT Act.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: There is no upper monetary cap on compensation NGT can impose; consumer forums have caps, not NGT.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: NGT cannot impose imprisonment for the pollution act itself. Imprisonment (up to 3 years) applies only when a party fails to comply with an NGT order, not as a sentence for committing the environmental violation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NGT can order both compensation and restoration simultaneously — these are not mutually exclusive remedies.

Value Addition:
• Criminal prosecution for the underlying environmental offence (e.g., under EPA 1986) proceeds separately through criminal courts.
• The 'polluter pays' principle is a statutory obligation on NGT under Section 20, not merely a judicial interpretation.
• If the company is a corporation, non-compliance with an NGT order can attract a fine of up to Rs. 25 crore.

solution.concept_anchor: Acts included in NGT Schedule I
solution.strong_distractor: d — The Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 sounds like an insurance/financial statute rather than an environmental law, leading some students to assume it does not belong in Schedule I and incorrectly selecting it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 — confirmed Schedule I Act; not the odd one out.
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 — confirmed Schedule I Act; not the odd one out.
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 — confirmed Schedule I Act despite its insurance-sector appearance; not the odd one out.
Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 — definitively NOT in Schedule I of the NGT Act; this is the odd one out — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 is the decoy odd one out — its name evokes insurance and finance rather than environmental law, making students dismiss it as out of place. Meanwhile, the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 sounds very much like an environmental statute, making it seem like a natural fit for Schedule I. The trap exploits the surface plausibility of WPA 1972 over PLIA 1991, when the statutory reality is the reverse.
solution.final_explanation:
Schedule I of the NGT Act defines the Acts under which NGT can exercise jurisdiction. Three of the four options belong to Schedule I; one does not.

• Option (a) — In Schedule I: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is a core scheduled Act.
• Option (b) — In Schedule I: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 is likewise a core scheduled Act.
• Option (c) — NOT in Schedule I: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 is the correct answer. Despite being a major environmental statute, it is excluded from Schedule I, meaning NGT cannot directly adjudicate disputes arising purely under WPA.
• Option (d) — In Schedule I: The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 is included, allowing NGT to deal with compensation claims related to industrial accidents involving hazardous substances.

Value Addition:
• For WPA 1972 matters, the appropriate forum remains the High Court (Art. 226) or the Supreme Court (Art. 32).
• NGT can still address wildlife-adjacent disputes if they involve Forest Conservation Act 1980 or EPA 1986 elements.
• The exclusion of WPA 1972 from Schedule I has been criticised by environmental lawyers as a significant jurisdictional gap.

Establishment and Constitutional/Statutory Basis of NGT

solution.concept_anchor: Section 20 NGT Act — precautionary principle as statutory obligation

statement_analysis.statement: Section 20 of the NGT Act imposes a statutory obligation on the NGT to apply principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and the polluter pays principle when adjudicating disputes.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 20 explicitly mandates these three principles as guiding norms — making them statutory obligations, not merely persuasive judicial tools.

statement_analysis.statement: The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle were first introduced into Indian environmental law through the NGT Act, 2010.
statement_analysis.reason: These principles were introduced into Indian environmental jurisprudence through judicial interpretation — notably the Supreme Court's landmark Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) judgment — well before the NGT Act was enacted.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Statement 1 is correct and are unaware that the Vellore Citizens case (1996) predated NGT may assume both statements are correct, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 20 of the NGT Act is explicit on this — all three principles are mandated; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Vellore Citizens case (1996) and later the A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu (1999) case introduced these principles through judicial interpretation — 14 years before the NGT Act 2010; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is temporal and attributive. Students who know that NGT enshrines the precautionary principle may jump to concluding that NGT introduced it into Indian law. In reality, the Supreme Court through the Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum case (1996) adopted these principles from international environmental law (Rio Declaration 1992) more than a decade before NGT existed. The NGT Act's innovation was codifying them as statutory obligations rather than leaving them as judicial innovations.
solution.final_explanation:
The precautionary principle's journey in Indian environmental law predates the NGT Act by over a decade, but the Act's contribution lies in making it a binding statutory norm for the tribunal.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 20 of the NGT Act 2010 mandates that the tribunal shall apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and the polluter pays principle. This statutory mandate means courts cannot ignore these principles when adjudicating — unlike before NGT, when their application depended on judicial discretion.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: These principles entered Indian environmental law through the Supreme Court's judgment in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), which drew upon the Rio Declaration 1992 (Principle 15 on precaution). The NGT Act 2010 codified what courts had already been applying judicially.

Value Addition:
• The Vellore case involved leather tanneries polluting the Palar River — it is the foundational precedent for precautionary and polluter pays principles in India.
• Rio Declaration 1992, Principle 15 is the international source of the precautionary principle.
• NGT's statutory codification of these principles means even a newly constituted bench has no discretion to exclude them — a significant advance over the pre-NGT position.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT non-compliance penalties — individual vs corporate fines
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) swaps the individual and corporate fine limits — Rs. 25 crore for individuals and Rs. 10 crore for companies — which sounds plausible since companies are typically larger entities liable for larger penalties.
elimination_logic: Recall the penalty framework: imprisonment up to 3 years for individuals for non-compliance — this is common to all options and is correct.
The individual fine cap is Rs. 10 crore — eliminate options citing different figures for individuals.
The corporate fine cap is Rs. 25 crore — higher than the individual cap, reflecting corporate accountability; confirm option (b).
Option (b) correctly states: individual fine up to Rs. 10 crore; corporate fine up to Rs. 25 crore — answer confirmed.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT Act prescribes a graduated penalty regime for non-compliance with its orders. The imprisonment and fine provisions serve as the enforcement backbone of the tribunal.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The fine for individual non-compliance is Rs. 10 crore, not Rs. 5 crore, and corporate liability is Rs. 25 crore, not Rs. 10 crore.
• Option (b) — Correct: For non-compliance by any person, the penalty is imprisonment up to 3 years, or a fine up to Rs. 10 crore, or both. If the non-compliant party is a company, the fine extends to Rs. 25 crore.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This reverses the figures — Rs. 25 crore applies to companies, not individuals; Rs. 10 crore applies to individuals, not companies.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The imprisonment period is 3 years, not 5 years. Five years is a figure associated with limitation periods for original applications, not imprisonment for non-compliance.

Value Addition:
• The imprisonment provision for non-compliance reinforces that NGT orders carry the weight of a civil court decree.
• NGT can transmit its orders to a Civil Court for execution as if they were decrees of that court — a key enforcement mechanism.
• The distinction between the pollution act (criminal law) and non-compliance with NGT orders (NGT Act penalty) is frequently tested.

concepts_used: NGT vs National Environment Appellate Authority (NEAA) — Predecessor Comparison

solution.concept_anchor: NEAA as predecessor to NGT — jurisdiction comparison
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who conflate the NEAA (1997) with the National Environment Tribunal Act 1995 may select option (b), thinking the NEAA predated both statutes and had broader jurisdiction than it actually did.
elimination_logic: Recall NEAA: established in 1997, had limited jurisdiction only over EIA-related approvals — this is the defining characteristic.
Evaluate option (a): NEAA — limited to EIA-related appellate jurisdiction. This is correct and precisely stated.
Evaluate option (b): NEAA did not have broader jurisdiction than NGT — it had a far narrower mandate; eliminate (b).
Evaluate options (c) and (d): Both misstate NEAA's role or establishment year; eliminate both — confirm (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The NEAA was a transitional body that preceded the NGT, and understanding its limitations explains why the NGT was needed.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: The National Environment Appellate Authority was established in 1997 under the NEAA Act and had jurisdiction confined to appeals against environmental clearances granted under the EIA Notification — an extremely narrow mandate. It lacked expert members, compensation powers, and the ability to handle diverse environmental disputes.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: The NEAA had narrower, not broader, jurisdiction compared to the NGT. Its restriction to EIA clearances was its principal limitation.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: The NEAA was not dissolved by the Environment Protection Act 1986 — it was superseded when the NGT Act 2010 came into force.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: The NEAA did not have expert members with scientific qualifications — this was one of the structural improvements the NGT introduced.

Value Addition:
• The National Environment Tribunal (NET), established under the NET Act 1995, was also subsumed into the NGT framework along with the NEAA.
• NGT's improvements over NEAA: expert members, broader Schedule I jurisdiction, compensation powers, restoration orders.
• The NEAA's sole focus on EIA appeals meant all other environmental violations had to be pursued through High Courts before the NGT was created.

Composition of NGT — Judicial and Expert Members

solution.concept_anchor: NGT bench quorum — mandatory expert member requirement

statement_analysis.statement: A bench of the NGT consisting solely of judicial members, without any expert member, is not validly constituted for hearing and deciding a case.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT Act requires every bench to have at least one Judicial Member and at least one Expert Member — a bench without an expert member is procedurally invalid, reflecting the tribunal's interdisciplinary mandate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairperson of the NGT has the power to constitute special benches for urgent or complex environmental matters.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chairperson retains administrative authority to constitute special or larger benches to address particularly urgent or technically complex disputes, ensuring flexibility in the tribunal's functioning.

statement_analysis.statement: An Expert Member of the NGT can independently adjudicate a case without the participation of any Judicial Member, provided the matter is purely technical in nature.
statement_analysis.reason: No provision in the NGT Act permits a bench composed exclusively of expert members. The quorum requirement for at least one judicial member is absolute — there is no 'purely technical' exception.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that expert members have real decision-making power (not merely advisory) may infer from this that they can act independently in technical matters, choosing option (c) which includes Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the mandatory expert member requirement is explicit in the Act; any option excluding Statement 1 is wrong.
Statement 2 is correct — the Chairperson's power to constitute special benches is a recognised administrative authority; retain options including Statement 2.
Statement 3 is incorrect — no 'purely technical' exception to the judicial member quorum exists; eliminate all options that include Statement 3.
Only option (d) — Statements 1 and 2 only — satisfies both conditions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap — it appeals to the intuition that technical matters should be decided by technical experts. The NGT's design is precisely the opposite: interdisciplinary adjudication requires both legal and scientific minds. The 'purely technical' exception does not exist, but students who appreciate the expert member's role may over-extend this to imply independent adjudicatory authority. The scope-extension is from 'expert members have substantive input' to 'expert members can adjudicate alone' — a step the statute never permits.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT's quorum rules are central to its interdisciplinary character. Every bench must combine legal and scientific expertise — neither alone suffices.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A bench without an expert member is not validly constituted. This is non-negotiable under the NGT Act, regardless of the simplicity or urgency of the matter.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Chairperson holds the administrative authority to constitute special or larger benches, enabling the tribunal to respond flexibly to urgent environmental crises or particularly complex technical disputes.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No provision in the NGT Act creates a 'purely technical matters' exception to the judicial member quorum. Expert members are co-adjudicators, not independent decision-makers. They examine technical reports, pollution data, and scientific evidence alongside the judicial member who applies the law.

Value Addition:
• The expert member's role includes directly evaluating pollution monitoring reports, baseline environmental data, and environmental impact assessments — unlike ordinary court proceedings where such reports must pass through expert witnesses.
• Chairperson can also direct a Zonal Bench to hear a matter if it arises in that bench's territorial jurisdiction.
• The interdisciplinary bench model reduces reliance on external expert witnesses, potentially speeding up environmental litigation.

concepts_used: Role of NGT in Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Disputes

solution.concept_anchor: NGT EIA jurisdiction — quash and remand, not substitute
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the NGT has EIA jurisdiction and can intervene in procedural violations may assume it can rewrite the EIA report itself, selecting (a) without appreciating the 'quash and remand' limitation.
elimination_logic: EIA notifications are issued under EPA 1986 — a Schedule I Act — so NGT has jurisdiction; confirm this before evaluating the scope of that jurisdiction.
Eliminate (a): NGT cannot substitute its own EIA assessment — this would usurp the role of the competent technical authority (MoEF&CC); the power is limited to quashing a flawed EIA and remanding.
Eliminate (c): NGT can examine procedural violations such as inadequate public hearing processes or flawed baseline data — this is within its jurisdiction.
Eliminate (d): NGT does not lack jurisdiction merely because an EIA involves a central government project; confirm (b) as the correct limitation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is a scope-extension of NGT's EIA powers. Students correctly learn that NGT has jurisdiction over EIA disputes (EPA 1986 is in Schedule I) and can intervene when there are procedural violations. The trap is the implicit extension to concluding that NGT can therefore rewrite or substitute the EIA with its own assessment. This is an executive function — the NGT's role is judicial review, not technical substitution. When it finds an EIA flawed, it quashes it and remands the matter to the competent authority for fresh consideration.
solution.final_explanation:
EIA notifications issued under the Environment Protection Act, 1986 fall squarely within Schedule I of the NGT Act, giving the tribunal jurisdiction to examine disputes arising from environmental clearances.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The NGT cannot prepare, rewrite, or substitute its own EIA in place of a flawed one. This would amount to exercising executive functions reserved for MoEF&CC or SEIAA. When an EIA is found procedurally deficient, the tribunal quashes the clearance and remands the matter for fresh consideration.
• Option (b) — Correct: The NGT can examine procedural violations in the EIA process — such as inadequate public hearings, flawed baseline data collection, or non-application of mind by the appraisal committee — and can quash the clearance and direct fresh proceedings.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: NGT does have jurisdiction to examine procedural infirmities — this is a well-settled aspect of its jurisdiction.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The involvement of a central government project does not divest NGT of jurisdiction; EIA clearances for central projects under EPA 1986 are equally subject to NGT oversight.

Value Addition:
• The Navi Mumbai Airport EIA challenge before NGT is a notable example of procedural violation scrutiny.
• MoEF&CC is the competent authority for Category A projects; SEIAA for Category B projects — both are subject to NGT appellate jurisdiction.
• 'Quash and remand' is the standard NGT remedy for flawed environmental clearances.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT interim orders — enforceability and standards

statement_analysis.statement: Interim orders of the NGT carry a lower penalty for non-compliance compared to final orders under the NGT Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Non-compliance with interim NGT orders attracts the same penalties as non-compliance with final orders — there is no two-tier penalty system; immediate enforceability is a key feature of NGT interim relief.

statement_analysis.statement: The standard applied by the NGT for granting interim relief is identical to that applied by civil courts — prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable harm.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT applies the same tripartite civil court standard for interim relief — this is a correctly stated standard and is not incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: The NGT can issue interim stay orders on construction activities in eco-sensitive zones even before hearing the opposing party, if circumstances so warrant.
statement_analysis.reason: Ex parte interim orders (without hearing the other side) are permissible where circumstances of urgency and irreparable harm are demonstrated — this is consistent with civil procedural law norms applied by NGT.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who suspect that interim orders may have lesser enforceability than final orders might choose only Statement 1 as incorrect, overlooking that the question asks which are NOT correct and that only Statement 1 qualifies.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The claim that interim orders carry a lower penalty is factually wrong — same penalties apply; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable harm is the standard — correctly stated; Statement 2 is correct, not the answer.
Evaluate Statement 3: Ex parte interim orders in urgent environmental cases are permissible under civil procedure norms; Statement 3 is correct, not the answer.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct → answer is (a). Wait — re-check options. The option listing only Statement 1 as incorrect is (a); confirm the answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets the intuitive assumption that interim orders — being provisional — might carry lesser legal weight or attract lighter penalties than final orders. The NGT Act does not create this distinction; an interim order is as binding and enforceable as a final order, and non-compliance with either attracts identical statutory penalties. This is important because it prevents parties from strategically ignoring interim orders while litigation continues.
solution.final_explanation:
NGT's interim powers are substantial — they operate immediately and with the full force of final orders until vacated.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: There is no graduated or lesser penalty for non-compliance with interim orders. Whether the order is interim or final, non-compliance attracts imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to Rs. 10 crore (Rs. 25 crore for companies). This design prevents dilatory non-compliance during the pendency of proceedings.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The NGT applies the well-established tripartite test from civil courts: (i) prima facie case in the applicant's favour, (ii) balance of convenience favouring the grant of interim relief, and (iii) irreparable harm if interim relief is refused.
• Statement 3 — Correct: In urgent environmental matters, ex parte interim orders — those passed without hearing the opposing party — are permissible. Courts and tribunals routinely pass such orders when urgency and irreparable harm are demonstrated, provided the opposing party is heard at the earliest opportunity thereafter.

Value Addition:
• Interim stay on construction in eco-sensitive zones is one of NGT's most impactful tools — it prevents fait accompli situations where construction is completed before the tribunal decides.
• Ex parte orders are typically valid for short periods and must be confirmed or vacated after the opposing party is heard.
• The immediate enforceability of NGT interim orders differentiates it from certain regulatory bodies whose directions can be ignored with only administrative consequences.

concepts_used: NGT's Power to Restore Environment — 'Restitution' Jurisdiction
Relief and Compensation Powers of NGT

solution.concept_anchor: NGT restitution jurisdiction — quasi-executive restoration powers
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may choose (b) if they question whether ecological restoration being 'beyond typical tribunal powers' explains why NGT is granted it by statute — leading them to think R explains something else about A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. NGT can order environmental restoration beyond monetary compensation and can create special funds for ecological repair — this is expressly provided in the NGT Act and represents quasi-executive power.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The polluter pays principle, as codified in Section 20 of the NGT Act, is the normative foundation requiring the entity causing environmental harm to bear the full cost of remediation, including ecological restoration.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The NGT's restoration powers are a direct expression of the polluter pays principle — it is because the polluter must bear all costs (not just victim compensation) that the NGT is empowered to order environmental restoration and create restoration funds.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → correct_option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
NGT's restitution jurisdiction extends the polluter pays principle from financial compensation into active ecological remediation — a powerful quasi-executive function not found in ordinary tribunals.

Assertion (A): Correct. Beyond awarding compensation to affected persons, the NGT is empowered to order restitution of damaged ecosystems, direct the creation of special restoration funds, and oversee remediation managed by designated authorities. This goes well beyond the typical tribunal's role of awarding money damages.

Reason (R): Correct. Section 20 of the NGT Act codifies the polluter pays principle as a statutory mandate. This principle holds that the entity causing environmental harm must bear the full cost of remediation — not just the costs borne by human victims but also the cost of ecological repair.

Causal link: R correctly explains A. The restoration jurisdiction flows logically from the polluter pays principle — if the polluter must pay for all harm caused, this necessarily includes the cost of restoring the environment to its pre-pollution state, not merely compensating human sufferers monetarily.

Value Addition:
• Compensation (to victims) and Restoration (ecological repair) are distinct remedies and can be ordered simultaneously by NGT.
• Special restoration funds are managed by designated authorities, not the NGT itself — this preserves the tribunal's adjudicatory role while executive implementation is handled elsewhere.
• This dual remedy mechanism mirrors international environmental law standards under treaties like the Nagoya Protocol and Superfund legislation in the USA.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological evolution of India's environmental tribunals
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places the National Environment Tribunal Act (1995) before the NEAA (1997) but incorrectly positions the NGT Act before the Rio Earth Summit, which would be factually impossible — students who know the NET-NEAA sequence but misremember the NGT year fall for this.
elimination_logic: The Rio Earth Summit (1992) preceded all domestic Indian legislative responses — place it first in any valid sequence.
The National Environment Tribunal Act was enacted in 1995 — after Rio 1992 but before NEAA 1997; second in sequence.
The NEAA was established in 1997 under the NEAA Act — third in the sequence.
The NGT Act was enacted in 2010 — last in sequence; only option (b) correctly orders: Rio 1992 → NET Act 1995 → NEAA 1997 → NGT Act 2010.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates on two levels. First, students may confuse 1995 (NET Act) and 1997 (NEAA) — both are 1990s statutes with similar environmental tribunal mandates. Second, some students who recall that NEAA was a 'predecessor' to NGT may place NEAA after the NGT Act in a narrative sense, when chronologically NEAA predates NGT by 13 years. The Rio 1992 anchor is the giveaway — any option placing it after 1995 is immediately eliminable.
solution.final_explanation:
India's dedicated environmental adjudication framework evolved in stages, each responding to international commitments and domestic gaps.

Correct sequence: Rio Earth Summit (1992) → National Environment Tribunal Act (1995) → National Environment Appellate Authority established (1997) → NGT Act (2010).

• Rio 1992: The Earth Summit's principles, including Principle 15 (precaution) and Principle 16 (polluter pays), created the normative impetus for specialised environmental law bodies in India.
• NET Act 1995: Created a framework for compensation for chemical accidents — a response to Bhopal's aftermath — though the tribunal itself was never fully operationalised.
• NEAA 1997: Established to hear appeals against EIA clearances; had very limited jurisdiction and no expert members.
• NGT Act 2010: Subsumed both NEAA and NET into a broader, multi-jurisdictional tribunal with expert members and compensation/restoration powers.

Value Addition:
• The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) is the background motivator for both the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 and the NET Act 1995.
• The NGT Act 2010 came into force on 18 October 2010.
• India's NGT is considered one of the most advanced dedicated environmental tribunals globally, often compared to Australia's Land and Environment Court (established 1980).

concepts_used: Relationship Between NGT and High Courts — Jurisdictional Overlap
Exclusion of Wildlife Protection Act and Its Implications

solution.concept_anchor: Forum selection — WPA matters and High Court writ jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know NGT has jurisdiction over forest matters (Forest Conservation Act 1980) may extend this to assume it also covers the Wildlife Protection Act 1972, choosing option (a) without recognising the critical distinction between the two statutes.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a challenge purely under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — identify whether WPA 1972 is a Schedule I Act.
WPA 1972 is NOT in Schedule I of the NGT Act — NGT has no direct jurisdiction over pure WPA matters; eliminate option (a).
High Courts retain writ jurisdiction under Art. 226 for matters under non-scheduled Acts including WPA 1972 — this is the correct forum; confirm option (c).

Eliminate (b): Supreme Court is not the appropriate first forum — writ petitions before High Courts are the standard route for WPA matters; eliminate (d) as NGT explicitly cannot take suo motu cognizance.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap conflates the Forest Conservation Act 1980 (which IS in Schedule I) with the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 (which is NOT). Both deal with biodiversity-adjacent matters, and the NGT frequently deals with forest-related disputes. Students who know that 'forest matters go to NGT' extend this incorrectly to wildlife protection matters. The critical distinction — which specific statute is invoked — determines jurisdiction entirely.
solution.final_explanation:
A wildlife activist challenges the grant of a mining licence in a wildlife sanctuary on the ground that it violates protections under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. She seeks to quash the licence.

Applicable principle: Jurisdiction before the NGT is limited to matters arising under the seven Acts in Schedule I. The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is not in Schedule I. For challenges purely under the WPA, the appropriate forum is the High Court through a writ petition under Article 226.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: NGT has no direct jurisdiction over disputes arising purely under WPA 1972. Selecting NGT here would result in a dismissal for want of jurisdiction.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: While the Supreme Court can be approached under Art. 32, a High Court writ under Art. 226 is the appropriate and conventional first recourse for WPA matters — it is more accessible and geographically proximate.
• Option (c) — Correct: The High Court's writ jurisdiction under Art. 226 is unaffected by the NGT Act and remains the primary forum for challenges under non-scheduled Acts like WPA 1972.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: NGT cannot take suo motu action — it requires a petition to be filed; even if NGT had jurisdiction (which it does not here), this option is doubly wrong.

Value Addition:
• If the mining licence also involves violations of the Forest Conservation Act 1980 or EPA 1986, NGT can be simultaneously approached for those aspects.
• Forum selection strategy — combining WPA (HC) and FCA 1980/EPA 1986 (NGT) challenges — is common in large infrastructure litigation.
• The Supreme Court has directed courts and tribunals to avoid jurisdictional overlap by clearly identifying which statute is the primary cause of action.

Original Jurisdiction of NGT

solution.concept_anchor: NGT suo motu absence contrasted with constitutional courts

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the Supreme Court of India, the National Green Tribunal cannot initiate proceedings on its own motion in response to reports of environmental violations.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT is entirely petition-driven and lacks suo motu power — this contrasts with the Supreme Court's power under Art. 32 to act on its own motion in matters involving fundamental rights, including the right to a healthy environment.

statement_analysis.statement: High Courts of India also cannot take suo motu cognizance of environmental violations, and are therefore similarly restricted to the same petition-driven model as the NGT.
statement_analysis.reason: High Courts do possess the power to take suo motu cognizance of environmental violations under Article 226 — this is a well-established practice; High Courts are NOT similarly restricted to a petition-driven model like the NGT.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as true may assume that the restriction on suo motu powers is uniform across all non-constitutional bodies, leading them to mark Statement 2 as correct also.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The absence of suo motu powers in NGT is well-established — it requires a petition to invoke jurisdiction; Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: High Courts under Art. 226 can and do take suo motu cognizance — this is an established practice in environmental PILs; Statement 2 equates High Courts with NGT's restriction, which is false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces the Supreme Court (clearly known to have suo motu power) with High Courts in Statement 2. Students who know the NGT-Supreme Court contrast well may not immediately recall that High Courts under Art. 226 are equally empowered to initiate suo motu proceedings. The trap is the implicit grouping of all non-Supreme Court bodies as lacking suo motu powers — High Courts are constitutional courts and possess this power fully.
solution.final_explanation:
The presence or absence of suo motu jurisdiction is a crucial differentiator between constitutional courts and statutory tribunals.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The NGT operates on a petition-driven model exclusively. It cannot convert a newspaper report, a public interest letter, or its members' personal observations into a pending proceeding. This is a significant limitation given that environmental damage is often irreversible while the search for a petitioner who can file continues.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: High Courts, as constitutional courts exercising jurisdiction under Article 226, retain full power to take suo motu cognizance of environmental violations. Indian High Courts regularly register suo motu PILs based on newspaper reports, letters, or judicial notice of environmental crises — a practice that fills the gap left by NGT's absence of such powers.

Value Addition:
• The absence of suo motu powers in NGT has led critics to argue for an amendment to the NGT Act granting this power — particularly for time-sensitive ecological disasters.
• The Supreme Court has occasionally transferred suo motu environmental PILs from High Courts to the NGT for specialised adjudication once a petitioner is formally registered.
• Art. 226 gives High Courts a broader geographical jurisdiction (within their territorial limits) than Art. 32, which is confined to fundamental rights enforcement.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT penalty and compensation framework — correct parameter identification

statement_analysis.statement: The NGT can impose a fine on an individual for non-compliance with its orders that may extend up to Rs. 10 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT Act prescribes a fine up to Rs. 10 crore for non-compliance by any person (individual) — this figure is correctly stated.

statement_analysis.statement: The maximum fine for non-compliance by a company under the NGT Act is the same as for an individual — Rs. 10 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: The fine for non-compliance by a company is Rs. 25 crore — higher than the individual limit of Rs. 10 crore; equating them is a factual error.

statement_analysis.statement: The NGT is empowered to impose an upper monetary limit on the compensation it awards to pollution victims, similar to the limits applicable under the Consumer Protection Act.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no upper cap on compensation the NGT can award — this distinguishes it from consumer forums which have tiered monetary jurisdiction limits.

statement_analysis.statement: Imprisonment for non-compliance with NGT orders may extend up to 3 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 26 of the NGT Act provides for imprisonment up to 3 years for non-compliance — correctly stated.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Wait, (c) is the correct answer here. The strong distractor is (b) — 'Only two' — which tempts students who correctly identify Pairs 1 and 4 as correct but then mistakenly mark Pair 3 as correct, thinking NGT does have some internal limit structure.
elimination_logic: Pair 1 (Rs. 10 crore individual fine): Correctly stated — mark correct.
Pair 2 (same Rs. 10 crore for companies as individuals): Incorrect — company fine is Rs. 25 crore, not Rs. 10 crore — mark incorrect.
Pair 3 (NGT has monetary cap on compensation like consumer forums): Incorrect — no cap exists; NGT is explicitly uncapped unlike consumer forums — mark incorrect.
Pair 4 (imprisonment up to 3 years for non-compliance): Correctly stated — mark correct. Two correct pairs total → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pair 3 is the most subtle trap. Students who know consumer forums have jurisdictional monetary limits may assume all compensation-granting quasi-judicial bodies operate with similar caps. The NGT deliberately has no upper cap — this is one of its distinguishing features. A partially prepared student who is uncertain about the NGT's cap may mark Pair 3 as correct, inflating the count to three and choosing option (c) instead of the correct (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the NGT's penalty and compensation framework precisely is essential — the numbers and the presence or absence of caps are frequently tested.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Individual non-compliance fine up to Rs. 10 crore is correctly stated.
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: The corporate non-compliance fine is Rs. 25 crore — not the same as the individual fine of Rs. 10 crore. The higher corporate limit reflects the principle of enhanced corporate accountability.
• Pair 3 — Incorrect: The NGT has no monetary ceiling on compensation awards. This is in direct contrast to consumer forums (District, State, National) which have clearly defined pecuniary jurisdiction limits. The absence of a cap allows NGT to award compensation commensurate with actual environmental and human harm.
• Pair 4 — Correct: Imprisonment for non-compliance with NGT orders extends up to 3 years — correctly stated under Section 26 of the NGT Act.

Two pairs are correct → answer is (b) Only two.

Value Addition:
• Consumer Protection Act 2019 jurisdictional limits: District Commission up to Rs. 1 crore; State Commission Rs. 1–10 crore; NCDRC above Rs. 10 crore. NGT has no such tiering.
• The 3-year imprisonment provision makes NGT non-compliance a cognisable and significant deterrent.
• NGT can transmit its compensation orders to a Civil Court for execution as a decree — ensuring enforceability.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT Zonal Bench cities — Kolkata Eastern Bench
solution.strong_distractor: b — Pune sounds like it could be the 'Southern' Bench given Maharashtra's relative position on India's map, leading some students to doubt it and select it as the odd one out, when in fact Pune is the correct Western Bench location.
elimination_logic: New Delhi — confirmed Principal Bench; belongs to the NGT bench system.
Pune — confirmed Western Bench; belongs to the NGT bench system.
Chennai — confirmed Southern Bench; belongs to the NGT bench system.
Hyderabad — NOT a designated NGT bench location; Hyderabad falls under the Southern Bench (Chennai) jurisdiction; it is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Hyderabad is a major city, the capital of Telangana (and formerly Andhra Pradesh), and a significant industrial hub — one might expect it to host a dedicated NGT bench. The geographic-swap trap inserts Hyderabad as plausibly seeming like a regional bench location for South-Central India, while the actual Southern Bench covering Telangana and Andhra Pradesh is at Chennai. Students unfamiliar with the precise bench cities may eliminate Pune or Chennai instead.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT has four Zonal Benches plus the Principal Bench — knowing the exact cities is a standard exam requirement.

• Option (a) — New Delhi: This is the Principal Bench location — valid NGT bench city.
• Option (b) — Pune: This is the Western Bench — covers Maharashtra, Goa, Gujarat and surrounding states. Valid NGT bench city.
• Option (c) — Chennai: This is the Southern Bench — covers Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana. Valid NGT bench city.
• Option (d) — Hyderabad: Not a designated NGT bench location. Matters from Telangana and Andhra Pradesh are handled by the Southern Bench at Chennai. Hyderabad is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• The four Zonal Bench cities — Bhopal (Central), Pune (Western), Kolkata (Eastern), Chennai (Southern) — should be memorised as a set.
• Hyderabad's absence as a bench location despite being a major industrial city has been flagged by environmental lawyers in Telangana as an access-to-justice concern.
• NGT can hold Circuit Bench sittings at additional locations, including potentially Hyderabad, for the convenience of litigants — but it is not a permanent bench.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT-High Court jurisdictional coexistence and appellate bypass

statement_analysis.statement: The establishment of the NGT does not extinguish the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 in environmental matters — both forums can technically entertain such disputes.
statement_analysis.reason: The NGT Act does not oust High Court writ jurisdiction; Art. 226 is a constitutional provision and cannot be abrogated by ordinary legislation. However, the Supreme Court has directed parties to prefer NGT as the specialised forum for scheduled Act matters.

statement_analysis.statement: Appeals against NGT orders may be filed before the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the bench that passed the order is situated.
statement_analysis.reason: Appeals from NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court — no High Court review is contemplated, regardless of which Zonal Bench passed the order. This is expressly provided under Section 22 of the NGT Act.

statement_analysis.statement: For matters involving statutes not listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act, such as the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, High Courts are the appropriate forum through writ petitions.
statement_analysis.reason: High Courts retain jurisdiction over non-scheduled Act matters through Art. 226; the NGT's lack of jurisdiction over WPA 1972 leaves the writ route as the primary remedy for wildlife-specific challenges.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) includes Statement 2 (which says High Court appellate review is available), which is the most common misconception — students incorrectly assume the zonal nature of NGT benches creates a corresponding High Court appellate link.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: High Courts retain Art. 226 jurisdiction even post-NGT — this is a settled legal position; Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Section 22 of the NGT Act directs appeals to the Supreme Court directly — not to any High Court; Statement 2 is categorically incorrect; eliminate all options containing Statement 2 as correct.
Statement 3: WPA 1972 is excluded from Schedule I — High Court is the correct forum; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a very natural logical assumption: if there is a Zonal Bench of the NGT at Chennai (Southern), surely its orders would be appealable to the Madras High Court, just as tribunal orders typically go to the relevant High Court. This territorial logic is firmly rejected by the NGT Act — the rationale is that a national-level specialised tribunal requires a single apex appellate body (the Supreme Court), not 25 different High Courts creating divergent environmental jurisprudence.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT-High Court relationship involves two distinct dimensions: concurrent jurisdiction over scheduled matters, and the complete exclusion of High Courts from the appellate hierarchy over NGT orders.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 226 is a constitutional guarantee — Parliament cannot strip High Courts of writ jurisdiction through ordinary legislation. NGT's establishment creates a concurrent but preferred forum, not an exclusive one. The Supreme Court's direction to prefer NGT is a guideline, not a jurisdictional bar.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This is the most important point. Appeals from NGT orders — whether from the Principal Bench or any Zonal Bench — go directly to the Supreme Court under Section 22. The time limit is 90 days from the NGT order. No High Court, including those in whose jurisdiction a Zonal Bench sits, has appellate authority over NGT decisions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: For WPA 1972 and other non-scheduled Act matters, the High Court through Art. 226 is the primary forum. This is where wildlife sanctuary violations, species protection disputes, and similar matters must be adjudicated.

Value Addition:
• The direct-to-Supreme-Court appeal route prevents 'bench hunting' across High Courts for favourable environmental jurisprudence.
• High Courts have, in some instances, heard NGT-related matters under Art. 226 to challenge NGT's jurisdiction itself — a meta-jurisdictional layer.
• Section 22 of the NGT Act 2010 is the specific provision governing the 90-day appeal window to the Supreme Court.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT original vs appellate limitation periods
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) correctly gives the original application period as 5 years but swaps the appellate period to 90 days (confusing it with the Supreme Court appeal period), which is a plausible-sounding figure from the same statutory framework.
elimination_logic: Recall the two limitation regimes: original applications under Section 14 have a 5-year limit.
Appellate applications under Section 16 have a 30-day primary limit (extendable by 60 more days) — not 90 days; 90 days is the Supreme Court appeal window.
Eliminate (a): 90 days is the Supreme Court appeal period, not the NGT appellate application period.
Confirm (b): 5 years for original applications; 30 days (extendable by 60 days) for appellate applications — correctly stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works by exploiting the proximity of three limitation-related numbers: 30 days (NGT appellate), 60 days (extension), 90 days (Supreme Court appeal from NGT). A student who recalls '90 days' in the NGT context but misidentifies its target (Supreme Court appeal vs NGT appellate application) will confuse the two and select option (a). The key is recognising that 90 days applies to the NEXT level up — the Supreme Court — not to the appellate filing before the NGT itself.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT operates under two distinct limitation regimes depending on whether the matter is an original application or an appeal.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: While 5 years for original applications is correctly stated, 90 days is not the appellate limit before NGT — 90 days is the window to appeal from NGT to the Supreme Court under Section 22.
• Option (b) — Correct: Original applications must be filed within 5 years of the cause of action arising (Section 14). Appellate applications must be filed within 30 days of the impugned order, with the tribunal empowered to condone delay for up to a further 60 days upon showing sufficient cause (Section 16).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A 3-year original application period does not exist in the NGT Act; 3 years is the imprisonment period for non-compliance.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Reversing the periods — 30 days for original and 5 years for appellate — is the opposite of the correct position, and would be structurally illogical since original disputes need longer windows than targeted appeals.

Value Addition:
• The 5-year original limitation is generous compared to civil courts' typical Article 113 (3-year) limitation — reflecting that environmental harm often manifests slowly.
• The NGT has discretion to condone delay beyond 30+60 days for appellate applications in exceptional circumstances.
• Confusion between 30 (NGT appellate), 60 (extension), 90 (SC appeal) is one of the most commonly exploited traps in NGT questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 48A and Article 21 as NGT philosophical basis
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Art. 21 has been interpreted to include the right to a healthy environment may choose (a), not realising that Art. 21 alone is not the complete answer — Art. 48A (DPSP) is equally foundational and should be paired with it.
elimination_logic: Art. 21 alone (option a): While the Supreme Court has read environmental rights into Art. 21, this is only part of the philosophical foundation — Art. 48A as a DPSP is equally relevant; eliminate (a) as incomplete.

Arts. 48A and 21 together (option b): Art. 48A directs the State to protect the environment (DPSP); Art. 21 protects life and personal liberty extended to include a healthy environment — both are the dual philosophical pillars; confirm (b).
Art. 32 alone (option c): Art. 32 is the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction — it is not an NGT enabling provision; eliminate (c).

Art. 253 (option d): Art. 253 enables Parliament to legislate for implementing international treaties — while it could technically support NGT Act as implementing Stockholm/Rio, it is not the stated philosophical underpinning; eliminate (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two distinct constitutional provisions (Art. 21 and Art. 48A) into one incomplete answer or separates them when both should be cited together. A student who knows Art. 21 encompasses environmental rights but is unaware of Art. 48A's explicit direction on environment protection will select (a) — factually true but incomplete. Option (b) correctly pairs both, representing the full philosophical scaffolding of the NGT.
solution.final_explanation:
The NGT's statutory existence is grounded in the NGT Act 2010, but its philosophical legitimacy in the Indian constitutional framework rests on two pillars.

• Option (a) — Incomplete: Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty) has been expanded by the Supreme Court to include the right to a wholesome environment. However, citing Art. 21 alone misses the explicit Directive Principle mandate.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 48A (Directive Principle) explicitly directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife — it is the most direct constitutional basis for environmental legislation. Article 21's judicial expansion to include environmental rights provides the fundamental rights dimension. Together, they form the philosophical foundation of the NGT.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 32 is the Supreme Court's power to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights — it is a jurisdiction-granting provision for the Supreme Court, not an NGT philosophical underpinning.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 253 enables Parliament to make laws implementing international treaties. While India's international commitments (Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992) did influence the NGT, Art. 253 is not the cited philosophical underpinning.

Value Addition:
• Art. 48A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment 1976, following the Stockholm Conference 1972.
• Art. 51A(g) — a Fundamental Duty — also directs citizens to protect the natural environment, adding a citizen-side constitutional basis.
• The Vellore Citizens case (1996) is the landmark that read Art. 21 together with Art. 48A to create a comprehensive constitutional environmental framework.
